system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2143-10-24 16:22:00 to 2143-10-26 18:15:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a complex medical history including type 1 diabetes, kidney transplant, chronic systolic and diastolic heart failure, complete heart block, and prior infections was admitted for replacement of a failing abdominal pacemaker generator. He underwent successful explant of the abdominal device and implantation of a Micra leadless pacemaker via the right femoral vein. Post-procedure, he experienced transient groin bleeding managed with manual pressure, intractable nausea attributed to gastroparesis and opioid use, and temporary urinary retention requiring catheterization. He recovered well, tolerated oral intake, ambulated without issue, and was discharged home with prophylactic antibiotics, activity restrictions, and follow-up in the device clinic. His heart failure and transplant medications were maintained throughout.

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  Chest radiograph

INDICATION:  History: ___ with recent pacer placement and explant of abdominal
generator with bleeding.  Evaluate hardware placement.

TECHNIQUE:  Portable AP radiograph view of the chest.

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph dated ___.

FINDINGS: 

Lung volumes have improved.  Position of pacer leads on this frontal view exam
appear unchanged.  The leadless pacer generator device projects over the left
lower mid hemithorax, similar to the prior exam when accounting for
differences in projection and inspiratory volumes.  Cardiomegaly persists,
unchanged.  Mild interstitial edema has markedly improved with residual
minimal pulmonary vascular congestion.  Slight blunting of the costophrenic
angles suggests trace bilateral small pleural effusions.  No focal parenchymal
opacities to suggest focal pneumonia.  No pneumothorax or evidence of
pneumomediastinum.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  Similar appearance of hardware placement on AP projection.
2.  Persisting cardiomegaly with trace bilateral pleural effusions but
interval resolution of mild interstitial edema.
3.  No focal pneumonia.

conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were just brought in from home because of bleeding near your pacemaker site. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Doctor. I got home yesterday after that pacemaker surgery, and this morning I started feeling pain in my belly. Then I noticed the bandage was wet with blood. It kept oozing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And did you have any coughing or hiccups recently? Sometimes that can strain the area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had hiccups all day and a bit of coughing. Could that have caused it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might have. The pressure from coughing or hiccups can reopen small blood vessels. We examined you and found a hematoma — that’s a collection of blood — under the incision from where your old pacemaker generator was removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if it keeps growing. But we’re going to take care of it. You’ll need a minor procedure to drain the blood and stop the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another procedure? I just had surgery yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. This one is much smaller. We’ll do it under local anesthesia. We’ll open the site slightly, remove the clot, and cauterize the bleeding spot. It should help you heal faster.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as it stops the bleeding. My belly feels tight and sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. We removed about 30 mL of clotted blood and cauterized a small bleeding vessel. The site is now clean and has a new pressure dressing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is the pacemaker still working? The new one in my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. The Micra pacemaker is inside your heart and wasn’t touched. The surgery today was only on the old abdominal generator site, which is now gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried something went wrong with the new device.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the device is fine. A chest X-ray confirmed the Micra is in the right place. Your heart rhythm looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other medicines? I take a lot for my diabetes, heart, and transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed all your meds. You’re on insulin, tacrolimus for your kidney transplant, heart meds like carvedilol and furosemide — all are continuing as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the aspirin? I was told to stop it before surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’re restarting aspirin today. Since the bleeding is controlled, it’s safe to resume it to protect your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. What about antibiotics? I’ve had infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. You’re on cephalexin — that’s Keflex — three times a day for one week to prevent infection at the surgical site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken that before. I’m allergic to Bactrim, just so you know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We have your allergies: Bactrim, Reglan, and sevoflurane. You’re safe with Keflex.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The pain is less, and no more bleeding. I’m hungry — can I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can start with light food. Given your gastroparesis, we’ll start with something easy to digest, like toast and applesauce.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My stomach has been slow for years, so I’m used to small meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your blood sugar closely. Your levels have been in the 190s — a bit high, but expected after surgery. Your insulin doses are continuing as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I check it at home every day. I’ll keep doing that when I go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep weighing yourself daily. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds in two days — that could mean fluid buildup from heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. My heart isn’t pumping as well as it should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. Your ejection fraction is around 40%, so we need to stay on top of fluid balance. But today, you look euvolemic — that means no fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the pressure dressing on for one full week. No heavy lifting or strenuous activity for seven days. And finish all the Keflex — even if you feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See the device clinic in one week. They’ll check the Micra and remove the dressing. Also keep seeing your cardiologist, nephrologist, and transplant team regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Final check: no fever, vitals stable, incision dry. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — take Tylenol for pain if needed. Avoid ibuprofen or other NSAIDs; they can affect your kidney and transplant meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stick to Tylenol. And call if the site starts bleeding again or gets red.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Also call if you have shortness of breath, chest pain, or dizziness. Otherwise, rest and take it easy. You’ve been through a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get home safely, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a complex medical history including type 1 diabetes, kidney transplant, chronic heart failure, complete heart block, and prior infections was readmitted one day after discharge due to bleeding and pain at the abdominal incision site following explant of a pacemaker generator. He had recently undergone placement of a Micra leadless pacemaker and removal of the abdominal device. Examination revealed a hematoma at the incision site, likely aggravated by coughing and hiccups. He underwent successful evacuation of the hematoma and cauterization of the bleeding source. His postoperative course was stable, with controlled pain, no further bleeding, and resumption of aspirin. He continued all baseline medications, including immunosuppressants, heart failure, and diabetes therapies. He was discharged home with a pressure dressing, a one-week course of cephalexin, activity restrictions, and follow-up in the device clinic.
